comments.text: The menu's entry, from the loader's file table. Clears menu_stale, silences and sets up the SID (snd_init), draws the menu frame and points CIA 1 at the keyboard. When a part has left a resume address in $085D-$085E (an option that loaded an event and is waiting for it to come back), jumps there instead of showing the menu.

Shows the menu of nine options and runs the one chosen. Sets the resume address back to here first, so that a part that ends by returning to the loader comes back to the menu. Patches the number of joysticks into the text of option 5 and prints the nine lines in one inline call; adds YES over (NO) when the Summer Games 1 events are on.

The inline text of the menu, read by print_inline: the screen address, then "1) COMPETE IN ALL THE EVENTS" to "9) CLOSING CEREMONIES", with 1 lo hi moving the cursor to each line and 2 lo hi pulling in shared words from the string table.
The digit of option 5, "NUMBER OF JOYSTICKS n": menu_show writes the number of joysticks there as a character before printing.
When the Summer Games 1 events are on, prints YES over the NO of option 6.
Inline text: YES) written over NO) on line 6 when the Summer Games 1 events are on.
Lets the player pick one of the nine options (choose_option, the last choice remembered in menu_choice) and jumps to it through the table below: pushes the address minus one and returns.
Low bytes, minus one, of the nine options' code: compete in all, some or one event, practise, joysticks, Summer Games 1 events, world records, opening and closing ceremonies.
High bytes of the nine options' addresses minus one.
Option 8: loads and runs file 1, the opening ceremony (run_part), then shows the menu again.
Option 9: loads and runs file 2, the closing ceremony, then shows the menu again. The end of the competition jumps here too.
Option 5: switches the number of joysticks between 1 and 2.
Option 6: switches the Summer Games 1 events on or off (bit 7 of sg1_events).

Option 4, practice: marks practising, names all eight records CONTESTANT, sets one player, asks which event (pick_practice) and runs it, then clears the player count and the practice mark. Practice never reaches the results screen, so a practice score is never shown, given a medal or saved as a record.
Option 3, one event: takes the names (get_players), asks "COMPETE IN WHICH EVENT?", shuffles the order of play, clears the scores, runs the event and shows its results.
Inline text: "COMPETE IN WHICH EVENT?".
Shuffles the players, clears the scores, takes the event, runs it and shows the results.
Option 1, every event: takes the names, selects all eight events (all sixteen with the Summer Games 1 events on) and goes on to the competition.

The competition, for options 1 and 2: runs the opening ceremony (file 1), then for each event whose bit is set in events_lo/events_hi, in menu order, clears the scores, runs the event and shows its results; between events shows the medal table (show_medals) and shuffles the order of play. After the last event works out each player's points from their medals, sorts the players by them and holds the champion ceremony, then runs the closing ceremony.
Inline text: "FINAL STANDINGS:".

The champion ceremony on the FINAL STANDINGS screen: starts the final standings' tune (number 6), then shows the players' lines one at a time from last place up to the champion, each after a pause from the tables below; then the champion's flag and anthem (show_winner).
The pause before the first line of the champion ceremony, by number of players less one, in units of about 74 frames.
The pause between the lines of the champion ceremony, by number of players.
Waits until fire has been released, then A times two frames or until fire is pressed.
Waits A times 74 frames with the tune playing (two calls of tune_step each frame); A = 0 returns at once.

Option 2, some events: takes the names, lists the events with DONE below them and lets the player switch each on and off; the chosen ones show in a second colour. DONE starts the competition when at least one event is chosen, else goes back to the menu.
Inline text: "SELECT THE EVENTS TO COMPETE IN".
No events chosen yet; lists them in blue (pick_list).
Inline text: "DONE" below the list of events.
The list's loop: the pointer moves over the events and DONE (choose_option); fire on an event switches its bit and redraws it, white when chosen and blue when not.
The bit of each of events 0 to 7 in events_lo.
The bit of each event in events_hi: none for events 0 to 7, then events 8 to 15 (the Summer Games 1 events).
Option 7, world records: lists the eight events with each record holder's name and score from the records page, plays the world records' tune (number 7) over and over and waits for fire.
Inline text: "WORLD RECORDS:".
Prints each of the eight events: its name and a colon, the spaces from event_pad, the holder's name, a space and the score.
Saves the caller's return address as the menu's resume address and starts the name entry; once the players are confirmed, the loader restarts the menu, which carries on from that address.
Prints "NEXT EVENT:" and the event's name, and waits 400 frames or until fire is pressed.
Inline text: "NEXT EVENT:".
Prints the event's name after it.
Shows the next event and loads and runs its file, the event number plus 4.

Loads and runs the file in X (the loader's $0903) after saving the caller's return address as the menu's resume address: the part ends by restarting the loader, the menu starts again and goes on from the caller.

Prints the text that follows the JSR, then returns past it. The text starts with the screen address, two bytes, and ends with 0; in it 1 lo hi moves the cursor and 2 lo hi prints another string from that address.
Reads the next byte of text at text_ptr, moves the pointer on and sets the flags by the byte.
Moves text_ptr on a byte and sets the flags by A; print_inline enters here to step from the JSR's last byte to the text.
Prints a space, keeping A.
LDY #$01, an entry that prints in white; nothing calls it.
Writes A at screen_ptr and text_colour at the same place in colour RAM (the high byte EORed with $DC turns $04-$07 into $D8-$DB), and moves the pointer on.
Prints character $D4 in red, the mark before each name in a list.

Clears the screen for a menu page: black border, cyan background, blue as the second multicolour, white text, the sprites off, multicolour text and the charset at $2000; fills the screen with character 0 in cyan, draws the white top and bottom rows and the striped bar on row 2.
Prints the world record holder's name for event_now, 10 characters from the records page.
Prints X characters from the address in A (high) and Y (low).
Prints the name of event_now (or of event X from print_event_x) from the string table.
Prints the name of event X.
Prints the string at A (high) and Y (low), with the same codes as print_inline.
The codes of a string: 1 lo hi moves the cursor, 2 lo hi prints the string at that address and comes back, any other byte is a character.
Prints the string at X (low) and Y (high).
Prints characters until the 0 that ends the string.
The offset of each event's record on the records page, 20 bytes each.
Prints the world record's score for event_now, 6 characters from offset 11 of its record.
The medal table between events: works out the points (score_medals), sorts, and lists every player with gold, silver, bronze and total.
Inline text: "COMPETITOR         G  S  B  TOTAL".
Lists every player with their medals and total, a row each.
Prints the mark and then player line_player's name and country, 16 characters.
Prints a space and the 6 characters of the score text.
Prints the player's gold, silver and bronze counts and then the total points, two digits each.
Works out each player's points from their medals: 5 for a gold, 3 for a silver and 1 for a bronze, into the score.
Prints two spaces and then the total as two digits.
Prints a space and A as two decimal digits, a leading zero as a space.
Gives the player in place 0, 1 or 2 (place) a gold, silver or bronze and prints its name, unless the score is zero: a fault wins nothing.
Low bytes of the GOLD, SILVER and BRONZE strings.
High bytes of the addresses of GOLD, SILVER and BRONZE.
Clears the screen and prints "PRACTICE WHICH EVENT?".
Inline text: "PRACTICE" then the rest of "WHICH EVENT?" from opt_one's text.
Lists the events and lets the player pick one into event_chosen and event_now.
Lists events A) to H), or A) to P) with the Summer Games 1 events on.
Prints one line of the list: the letter, ") " and the event's name, double-spaced for eight events and single-spaced for sixteen.
"CONTESTANT" and six spaces, the name and country field of every record in practice.
Clears the medals; takes new names (enter_names) unless there are players already, in which case asks "IS THIS CORRECT?" and takes new names on NO.
Lists the players' names and countries under "IS THIS CORRECT?" with A) YES and B) NO, and returns the choice in X.
Inline text: "IS THIS CORRECT?".
Prints the first answer.
Inline text: "A)  YES".
Prints the second answer.
Inline text: "B)  NO".
Lists the players' names and countries below the answers, then waits for the choice.
Zeroes the gold, silver and bronze counts of all eight records.
Zeroes the score of all eight records and fills their score text with spaces.

Low bytes of the names of the sixteen events in menu order, the eight of this game and then the eight of the first: Triple Jump, Rowing, Javelin, Equestrian, High Jump, Fencing, Cycling, Kayaking, then Pole Vault, Platform Diving, 4x400m Relay, 100m Dash, Gymnastics, Freestyle Relay, 100m Freestyle and Skeet Shooting.
High bytes of the event names' addresses, in the same order.
The event names, each ending in 0 (character $B8 is a small m), then WORLD RECORD.
The spaces after each event's name in the world records list, so that the names of the holders line up.
GOLD, SILVER and BRONZE, then the shared words of the menu: ") COMPETE IN ", "ONE EVENT", "ING CEREMONIES" and "PRACTICE ".

The results of an event: sorts the players by score, writes FAULT for a score of zero, checks for a new world record, then lists every player with their score and medal, places tied on the same score getting the same medal, and ends with the winner's flag and anthem.
Inline text: "CONTESTANTS        SCORE".
Lists the players in order of score: the mark, the name, the score and the medal, a tie with the player above keeping the same place.
Draws the flag of the first player's country, plays its anthem with the flag waving and waits for fire.
Waves the flag: for the band of lines from $4D to $8D sets a white background and the flag's colour, steps the tune twice a frame, and goes on for at least 60 frames and until the tune ends.
Compares the score of the record at X with the next one's; equal means a tie.
For each player turns a final M of the score text into the small m (character $B8), and writes " FAULT" for a score of zero.

When the winner's score, for one of this game's eight events, is at least the world record, shows the old and new records, copies the name and score into the records page and saves it to the disk (ldr_save_records).
Prints "NEW WORLD RECORD FOR" the event, then "OLD WORLD RECORD:" with the old holder and score and "NEW WORLD RECORD:".
Inline text: "NEW WORLD RECORD FOR ".
Prints the name of the event whose record was beaten.
Inline text: "OLD WORLD RECORD:".
Prints the old holder's name and score.
Inline text: "NEW WORLD RECORD:".
Returns to check_record, which prints the new holder and score.
Draws the flag of country Y in the middle of the screen: sets its two colours from flag_colours and copies 5 rows of 10 characters and their colours from the flag tables.
Copies 5 rows of 10 bytes from text_ptr to screen_ptr, rows 78 bytes apart in the tables and 40 on the screen.
Where each country's flag starts in the character tables, low bytes, by country number (row times 8 plus column of the flag picker).
High bytes of where each flag starts in the character tables.
Where each flag starts in the colour tables, low bytes.
High bytes of where each flag starts in the colour tables.

The two shared colours of the flags, by country number, one in each nibble for $D022 and $D023: the same for every flag of a band (blue and red for the first, yellow and red for the second, light blue and yellow for the third).
Sorts the players by score, highest first, swapping whole records.
Shuffles the order of play: swaps each record with one picked at random.
Swaps the records at X and Y, bytes $00 to $1C.
The RTS of swap_records, read as the entry before rec_offsets so that a player number counted from 1 finds its record.
The offset of each player's record, 32 bytes apart.
A random player number, below players.
The random number generator: shifts a 16-bit register in rnd_lo and rnd_hi and mixes in a counter. Called once a frame by read_stick too.
Lets the player choose between the two answers A) and B).
Lets the player choose an event from the list.

Moves a sprite pointer up and down a list with the joystick, repeating while it is held, and takes the choice on fire; a key with the option's number or letter picks it at once. A is the last option, X where the pointer starts and Y the screen line of the first. Returns the choice in X.
Waits until fire is released and no key is pressed for 15 frames.
Puts the pointer sprite by option cursor_pos.
Code nothing calls: waits for fire to be released and then pressed.
Screen offsets of the lines of an eight-line list, two rows apart, low bytes.
High bytes of the eight-line list's screen offsets.
Screen offsets of sixteen lines, one row apart, low bytes.
High bytes of the sixteen lines' screen offsets.

Waits for the next frame (raster line $FA then $FB), steps the random numbers and reads both joysticks together, keeping a reading only when it is the same two frames running. Returns Z set when fire is held.
Waits for raster line A.
Tune 17, Denmark's anthem. Each tune is rows of four bytes: the note numbers of the three voices and the row's length, ending at a byte of $80 or more.
Tune 1, France's anthem.
Tune 0, the anthem of the United States.
Tune 2, Great Britain's anthem.
The SID frequency of each note number, low bytes.
The SID frequency of each note number, high bytes.
The length of a row of a tune, in calls of tune_step, by the fourth byte of the row.
Clears the SID, sets the three voices' envelopes and pulse widths and the volume, and marks no tune playing.
Starts the tune of country Y (or numbers 6 and 7, which no country has: the final standings' tune and the world records' tune) unless one with a lower number is playing.
The tune for each country number, times 2, an index into the tune table at $3280.

Plays the tune, called twice a frame: counts down the row's length, releases the notes near its end, and at its end starts the next row's three notes (pulse waves on voices 1 and 2, a sawtooth on voice 3). A row starting with $80 or more ends the tune.
Silences the three voices and marks no tune playing.
Tune 12, Spain's anthem.
Tune 15, Norway's anthem.
Two zero bytes after the last tune.
The menu's character set, used by every menu page: the letters and digits in ASCII order, the frame and the bars, and the pieces of the eighteen flags.

The upper half of the character set from character $80: more pieces of the flags, the small m ($B8), the white top and bottom rows ($B9 and $BA), the stripes of the bar ($BB) and the mark before names ($D4).

The character tables of the flag picker, a screen row each, 78 bytes long: six flags 13 characters apart, read in a circle as the flags scroll. Three bands of flags, five rows of picture and a row of names each, their colours in the tables from $2C24. This is row 2 of the screen, the top row of the first band.
Row 3, the first band's second row of pictures.
Row 4, the first band's third row.
Row 5, the first band's fourth row.
Row 6, the first band's bottom row.
The names of the first band of flags: U.S.A., FRANCE, G. BRITAIN, W. GERMANY, AUSTRIA, ITALY.
Row 10, the second band's top row.
Row 11, the second band's second row.
Row 12, the second band's third row.
Row 13, the second band's fourth row.
Row 14, the second band's bottom row.
The names of the second band: U.S.S.R., CANADA, MEXICO, SPAIN, DENMARK, AUSTRALIA.
Row 18, the third band's top row.
Row 19, the third band's second row.
Row 20, the third band's third row.
Row 21, the third band's fourth row.
Row 22, the third band's bottom row.
The names of the third band: JAPAN, NETHERLANDS, EPYX, NORWAY, IRELAND, BRAZIL.
The colour tables of the flag picker, one for each row of pictures above, 78 bytes each. This is row 2's.
The colours of row 3.
The colours of row 4.
The colours of row 5.
The colours of row 6.
The colours of row 10.
The colours of row 11.
The colours of row 12.
The colours of row 13.
The colours of row 14.
The colours of row 18.
The colours of row 19.
The colours of row 20.
The colours of row 21.
The colours of row 22.
Ten zero bytes before the sprites.
Seven sprites: the pointer that marks a choice in the menus ($C3) and the six of the frame around the flag being chosen ($C4 to $C9).
The addresses of the twenty tunes: the eighteen anthems and tunes 6 and 7.
The table read one byte on, for the high byte of each tune's address.
Tune 16, Ireland's anthem.
Tune 14, Epyx's own tune for the country EPYX.
Tune 19, played over the world records.
Tune 13, Brazil's anthem.
Tune 7, West Germany's anthem.
Tune 8, Australia's anthem.
Tune 6, Japan's anthem.
Tune 3, the anthem of the Soviet Union.
Tune 4, Canada's anthem.
Tune 5, Mexico's anthem.
Tune 18, played over the final standings.
Tune 9, the anthem of the Netherlands.
Tune 10, Austria's anthem.
Tune 11, Italy's anthem.

The name entry: clears its zero page, draws the screen and the three bands of flags, starts the raster interrupts and the sprites, then each frame redraws the flags, flashes the frame, runs the entry's steps and moves the flags with the joystick.
Turns on the six sprites of the frame around the flag being chosen: expanded, black, from the positions below.
The six sprites' positions and the high bits of their X.
The six sprites' pointers, $C4 to $C9.
Turns off CIA 1's interrupt and sets the raster interrupt at line $FB through irq_entry.

The raster interrupt of the name entry: runs the handler for this slot from the tables below, then sets the next slot's line. Eight slots a frame change the background colours for the three bands of flags.
The raster line of each slot: $FB, $EB, $C0, $AB, $80, $78, $6C and $40.
High bytes of each slot's handler address minus one.
Low bytes of each slot's handler address minus one.
Line $FB: steps the tune and leaves the interrupt.
Black border, acknowledges the VIC and returns from the interrupt.
White background with blue and red for the first band of flags.
Black background between the bands.
White background with yellow for the second band.
White background with light blue and yellow for the third band.
Counts the frame, sets the frame flag the main loop waits for, and steps the tune a second time.
Zeroes $11 to $49.
Scans the keyboard and returns the key's character in A and key_code, $FF for none.
The row masks the keyboard scan writes to CIA 1.
The column bits.
The character of each key by row and column: DEL and RETURN in the first row, then the letters and digits.
Reads the columns of one keyboard row, returning $FF when a joystick is pulling lines low.

The steps of the name entry, by entry_state: 0 starts, 1 draws the heading for the next player, 2 takes the typing, 3 shows the name and "PICK YOUR COUNTRY", 4 the flags; with eight players, or a name left empty once there is one, the players are shown for "IS THIS CORRECT?": YES goes back to the menu through the loader, NO starts the names again.
An RTS nothing reaches.

Takes one key: RETURN ends the name, DEL rubs out a letter (repeating every 5 frames), and any other key adds it while the name is under 10 letters, a held key counting once. An empty name ends the entry once there is a player. The name and a space go into the record.
Drops a RETURN when the name typed is the same as an earlier player's.
Writes "PICK YOUR COUNTRY" on the top line with the player's name over the example name, and shows the frame.
The top line: "NELSON S.  PICK YOUR COUNTRY", the name overwritten by the player's.
The three letters of each country by number, XXX for the six numbers unused: USA, FRA, GBR, FRG, AUT, ITA, URS, CAN, MEX, ESP, DEN, AUS, JPN, HOL, EPX, NOR, IRL, BRA.
The table read one byte on, for the second letter of each code.
The table read two bytes on, for the third letter of each code.

Moves the flags with the joystick: left and right scroll the bands by one flag (13 characters over 13 frames) and change the column, up and down move the frame by one band (64 lines over 16 frames) and change the row, stopping at the top and bottom.
The column step for each joystick direction.
The frame's step in lines for each direction.
Moves the scroll position one character, in a circle of 78.
Moves the frame's sprites by frame_step lines.
Draws the three bands of flags and their colours from the scroll position: each row 40 characters from its 78-byte table, wrapping round.
Flashes the frame through the colours below; on the flags, waits for an anthem to end, then goes to the next player after a choice; S plays the country's anthem, fire chooses it.
The colours the frame flashes through.
Stores the country under the frame in the player's record, its number and "(XXX)", and returns the number in Y.
The name entry's screen: the charset, the flags scrolled to the start, the frame on France, then the heading.
Draws the colours and dividing lines of the screen and "#n ENTER YOUR NAME" with the player's number.
" #1 ENTER YOUR NAME" on a line of 40.
Rows of a tune that the tune table does not point at.
